news.content_title: UL45–46 Insertion Site in Herpesvirus Vector Enhances Chicken Protection
news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health UL45–46 Insertion Site in Herpesvirus Vector Enhances Chicken Protection Against H9N2 Influenza by November 26, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 UL45–46 Insertion Site in Herpesvirus Vector Enhances Chicken Protection Against H9N2 Influenza Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A recombinant vaccine using the herpesvirus of turkeys to express the hemagglutinin antigen of H9N2 avian influenza virus demonstrated superior immunogenicity and protective efficacy when targeted to the viral genome’s UL45–46 intergenic region rather than the conventional US2 locus. In controlled trials involving specific-pathogen-free chickens, in-ovo administration of the construct designated HVT-HAUL45–46 triggered significantly higher hemagglutination inhibition antibody titers and a substantially stronger antigen-specific cellular immune response than the comparative US2-vectored candidate. Following an experimental respiratory and ocular challenge with pathogenic H9N2 virus, chickens immunized with the UL45–46-engineered vector exhibited complete prevention of cloacal viral shedding, reduced oropharyngeal excretion, decreased lung viral loads, and preserved pulmonary tissue architecture. The H9N2 subtype of avian influenza virus has transitioned over several decades from a localized pathogen into an endemic operational hazard across poultry production systems in Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and sectors of Europe. While classified as a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus producing relatively mild clinical manifestations under isolated conditions, field infections within commercial poultry operations trigger significant declines in egg production, retard growth rates in broiler chickens, and impair feed conversion efficiency. Furthermore, H9N2 infection damages respiratory mucosal barriers and induces substantial immunosuppression, predisposing domestic flocks to severe secondary bacterial and viral coinfections with agents such as Escherichia coli and infectious bronchitis virus, which drive acute spikes in flock mortality. Beyond production agriculture, H9N2 viruses present persistent public health and pandemic threats due to their established role as internal gene donors during viral reassortment events. Multiple emergent avian strains capable of infecting mammalian hosts, including H7N9, H10N8, and H3N8, acquired their internal gene cassettes from circulating H9N2 lineages. Epidemiological monitoring reported by international health authorities documented sporadic human spillover infections involving H9N2 between 2024 and early 2025 across regions such as China and Bangladesh, with a pronounced frequency among pediatric cases. Molecular analyses trace these zoonotic spillover events to adaptive mutations in the viral hemagglutinin glycoprotein, underscoring the necessity of controlling H9N2 transmission directly at the poultry reservoir level. Conventional poultry vaccination programs predominantly utilize whole-virus inactivated oil-emulsion formulations, which reduce mortality and clinical symptoms but exhibit clear limitations in halting transmission cycles. Because H9N2 is a mucosal pathogen colonizing respiratory and intestinal tracts, parenteral delivery of inactivated vaccines fails to induce robust mucosal secretory immunoglobulin A responses or sustained cell-mediated immunity. Consequently, birds receiving standard inactivated vaccines continue to shed infectious virus into farm environments. Recombinant herpesvirus of turkeys (HVT) vectors represent an alternative strategy due to their established safety profile, ability to induce life-long persistent infection with continuous endogenous antigen presentation, and simultaneous activation of systemic and cell-mediated immune pathways. The double-stranded DNA genome of HVT contains multiple nonessential insertion regions within its unique long (UL) and unique short (US) domains, but the functional selection of an integration site fundamentally influences vector replication and foreign antigen expression. The US2 region has served as a standard integration site, having previously demonstrated higher antibody responses than the US10 locus. However, genetic alterations within the US domain can negatively affect viral fitness and T-cell stimulation. Conversely, the UL45–46 intergenic region has shown clinical utility in commercial Newcastle disease vectors. Molecular insights from related alphaherpesviruses indicate that the tegument protein UL46 acts as an innate immune antagonist by binding TANK-binding kinase 1 and preventing its dimerization, thereby suppressing the TBK1–IRF3 signaling axis and downstream type I interferon production. Targeted disruption or cassette placement at UL45–46 may relieve this innate immune inhibition, enhancing vector adjuvanticity and antigen processing. To directly assess comparative performance, researchers rescued the HVT-HAUL45–46 viral construct by applying CRISPR/Cas9 endonuclease cleavage to the parental HVT-FC126 genome at the UL45–46 locus, inserting an expression cassette encoding the hemagglutinin gene derived from the H9N2 strain A/chicken/Anhui/AH463/2017 through nonhomologous end joining. Flanking-primer polymerase chain reaction validated site-specific integration by distinguishing the extended recombinant amplicon from the parental sequence. Western blot analysis verified stable hemagglutinin expression at the expected molecular weight of approximately 70 kilodaltons, while indirect immunofluorescence assays confirmed cytoplasmic localization within infected primary chicken embryo fibroblasts. Serial in vitro propagation across 20 consecutive passages confirmed that the inserted gene cassette remained genetically stable without detectable deletions or sequence mutations. Multistep in vitro growth kinetics measured in chicken embryo fibroblasts over 120 hours revealed that the insertion of the foreign antigen cassette did not compromise vector replication viability. Although parental HVT viral titers exhibited slightly higher replication metrics at 72 and 120 hours post-infection, the overall growth curve of HVT-HAUL45–46 closely mirrored the parental virus. These data established that genetic insertion into the UL45–46 intergenic boundary preserves fundamental viral replication kinetics while stably retaining the heterologous avian influenza protective antigen across successive viral generations. In vivo comparative immunogenicity was evaluated in specific-pathogen-free chicken embryos vaccinated at embryonic incubation day 18.5 via amniotic cavity injection with 5000 plaque-forming units of either HVT-HAUL45–46, HVT-HAUS2, or phosphate-buffered saline control. Systemic humoral monitoring demonstrated that hemagglutination inhibition antibodies appeared by 7 days post-immunization and progressively increased through day 28 in both vaccinated cohorts. However, by 28 days post-vaccination, the HVT-HAUL45–46 cohort attained an average hemagglutination inhibition titer of 3.58 ± 0.54 log2, significantly surpassing the level elicited by the HVT-HAUS2 construct. While serum neutralizing antibody titers peaked early at day 7 and gradually declined without significant differences between the two vaccinated groups, both vector candidates stimulated local neutralizing antibody production in harderian gland homogenates, tracheal washes, and duodenal washes. This cellular response was significantly greater than the 243 ± 26 spot-forming cells per million recorded in the HVT-HAUS2 cohort, representing an approximate 2.8-fold elevation in interferon-gamma-secreting T lymphocytes. Unvaccinated control birds and sham-stimulated cultures exhibited virtually undetectable baseline responses, confirming the pronounced cellular stimulatory capacity associated with the UL45–46 locus. Protective viral clearance was verified by challenging vaccinated and control birds at 28 days post-immunization with 10^4 50% embryo infectious doses of H9N2 virus via combined intranasal and intraocular routes. In cloacal swab assessments performed at 3 and 5 days post-challenge, the HVT-HAUL45–46 vaccine completely prevented intestinal shedding, with zero out of ten birds shedding detectable virus at either time point. In contrast, the HVT-HAUS2 cohort exhibited cloacal shedding rates of 20 percent at day 3 and 40 percent at day 5, while the unvaccinated control group demonstrated 100 percent shedding. Oropharyngeal shedding was likewise attenuated; positive mucosal swabs in the HVT-HAUL45–46 group fell from 70 percent at day 3 to 60 percent at day 5, whereas the HVT-HAUS2 group recorded 90 percent and 80 percent shedding, and controls reached 100 percent positivity. Post-challenge lung examinations conducted at 5 days post-challenge demonstrated that both recombinant vaccines significantly lowered pulmonary viral loads relative to unvaccinated control birds. While quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction indicated lower mean viral titers in the HVT-HAUL45–46 cohort compared to HVT-HAUS2, this specific inter-vaccine titer difference did not achieve statistical significance. Histopathological evaluation via hematoxylin and eosin staining, however, revealed striking structural differences. Unvaccinated controls exhibited severe alveolar hemorrhage, vascular congestion, and marked inflammatory infiltration. Lungs from HVT-HAUS2-vaccinated chickens displayed moderate inflammatory lesions and pulmonary hemorrhage, whereas lung tissues from the HVT-HAUL45–46 cohort exhibited well-preserved tissue architecture with minimal inflammatory changes and substantially reduced vascular lesions. The collective experimental findings establish the UL45–46 intergenic junction as an advantageous insertion site for engineering herpesvirus-of-turkeys-vectored avian influenza vaccines. By sustaining high vector replication stability, generating elevated hemagglutination inhibition titers, eliciting potent splenic interferon-gamma cellular responses, and fully halting intestinal viral excretion, the HVT-HAUL45–46 construct addresses critical performance deficiencies inherent to conventional inactivated formulations and earlier recombinant designs. This platform presents an effective framework for advancing next-generation mucosal and cellular vaccines capable of interrupting H9N2 circulation within industrial poultry reservoirs. The H9N2 subtype of avian influenza virus has transitioned over several decades from a localized pathogen into an endemic operational hazard across poultry production systems in Asia, the Middle East, North Africa, and sectors of Europe. While classified as a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus producing relatively mild clinical manifestations under isolated conditions, field infections within commercial poultry operations trigger significant declines in egg production, retard growth rates in broiler chickens, and impair feed conversion efficiency. Furthermore, H9N2 infection damages respiratory mucosal barriers and induces substantial immunosuppression, predisposing domestic flocks to severe secondary bacterial and viral coinfections with agents such as Escherichia coli and infectious bronchitis virus, which drive acute spikes in flock mortality. Beyond production agriculture, H9N2 viruses present persistent public health and pandemic threats due to their established role as internal gene donors during viral reassortment events. Multiple emergent avian strains capable of infecting mammalian hosts, including H7N9, H10N8, and H3N8, acquired their internal gene cassettes from circulating H9N2 lineages. Epidemiological monitoring reported by international health authorities documented sporadic human spillover infections involving H9N2 between 2024 and early 2025 across regions such as China and Bangladesh, with a pronounced frequency among pediatric cases. Molecular analyses trace these zoonotic spillover events to adaptive mutations in the viral hemagglutinin glycoprotein, underscoring the necessity of controlling H9N2 transmission directly at the poultry reservoir level. Conventional poultry vaccination programs predominantly utilize whole-virus inactivated oil-emulsion formulations, which reduce mortality and clinical symptoms but exhibit clear limitations in halting transmission cycles. Because H9N2 is a mucosal pathogen colonizing respiratory and intestinal tracts, parenteral delivery of inactivated vaccines fails to induce robust mucosal secretory immunoglobulin A responses or sustained cell-mediated immunity. analysis.time: The study was published on November 26, 2026. The experimental trials were conducted with chickens vaccinated at embryonic incubation day 18.5, and the results were observed up to 28 days post-vaccination.
analysis.location_and_population: The research involved specific-pathogen-free chickens in controlled trials, with the H9N2 avian influenza virus as the target pathogen.
analysis.event: A recombinant vaccine using the herpesvirus of turkeys (HVT) to express the hemagglutinin antigen of H9N2 avian influenza virus was tested. The vaccine was targeted to the UL45–46 intergenic region of the HVT genome, showing superior immunogenicity and protective efficacy compared to the conventional US2 locus.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The H9N2 subtype is classified as a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus, but it causes significant declines in egg production, growth rates, and feed conversion efficiency in commercial poultry operations. It also predisposes flocks to severe secondary infections, which can lead to acute spikes in mortality. The study demonstrated that the UL45–46-engineered vector completely prevented cloacal viral shedding and reduced oropharyngeal excretion, with preserved pulmonary tissue architecture.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted using controlled trials and molecular analyses. The results were validated through flanking-primer PCR, Western blot, and indirect immunofluorescence assays. The findings are based on experimental data and are not yet applied in field settings. The research is part of a broader effort to develop more effective vaccines against H9N2.

analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该研究涉及无特定病原体的鸡进行对照试验,以 H9N2 禽流感 病毒为目标病原体。

news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Bird Flu Returns to Poland’s Turkey Farms as France Reports a New H5N1 Outbreak By Elias Reed Published: Nov 24 2026, 5:39 AM EST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Alex Rusin From PEXELS Highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu has struck a commercial turkey farm in northeastern Poland, the first such outbreak in the country in about six months. France has also reported a new farm outbreak in its north, as Europe enters the time of year when the virus usually spreads fastest. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), citing reports from national authorities, confirmed both outbreaks on Monday, 23 November 2026. Neither outbreak has been linked to any human infection. But together they show how quickly the virus can reach farms once autumn bird migration is under way, and why governments are tightening rules on keeping poultry indoors. The Polish outbreak The Polish case was found on a farm in Lipinki, in the Biskupiec commune of the Warmian-Masurian region, according to Polish broadcaster TVN24. The farm raised more than 18,700 turkeys for slaughter. The provincial veterinary inspectorate in Olsztyn received laboratory results on Monday. Samples were tested at Poland's National Veterinary Research Institute in Puławy, which detected genetic material of the H5N1 avian influenza virus. According to Reuters, WOAH said 587 of the farm's 18,723 birds died, and the rest were culled. The inspectorate said procedures to eradicate the disease had been put in place. Local officials in Biskupiec urged residents to keep poultry and other domestic birds indoors and to follow the veterinary service's guidance. WOAH said this was Poland's first outbreak of highly pathogenic H5N1 in six months. That matters well beyond one farm. Poland is the European Union's largest poultry exporter, so outbreaks there can trigger trade restrictions and affect supply chains across the region. France confirms a northern case In France, the virus hit a poultry farm in the Pas-de-Calais area in the north of the country, Reuters reported, again citing WOAH. The disease killed 80 of the farm's 4,300 birds, and the remaining birds were culled. The report did not say what species the farm kept. The outbreak was detected the previous Thursday. A day later, France raised its national bird flu risk level to "high," the top tier, which brings rules such as keeping poultry confined indoors. TVN24 also noted France's move to its highest risk level. The details of the French outbreak in this article rest on the Reuters report of WOAH's notification. French authorities' own notice was not reviewed. Why autumn brings more outbreaks Bird flu outbreaks in Europe follow a strong seasonal pattern. As autumn arrives, millions of ducks, geese and swans migrate south and west from breeding grounds in northern Europe and Siberia. Wild waterbirds can carry avian influenza viruses, sometimes without showing signs of illness, and spread them along their routes. Farms become infected when the virus passes from wild birds into poultry houses. That can happen through direct contact with birds outdoors, through droppings on feed or water, or on boots, vehicles and equipment that move between areas. Once inside a large flock, a highly pathogenic strain can spread fast. Turkeys and chickens are especially vulnerable and often die in large numbers. This is why the standard response is so severe. When a highly pathogenic strain is confirmed, authorities usually cull the whole flock, clean and disinfect the site, and set up control zones around the farm with restrictions on moving birds and products. The Polish report did not give the size of any zones around the Lipinki farm. What it means for wild birds H5N1 is not only a farm problem. Since the early 2020s, the strain circulating widely around the world has killed large numbers of wild birds, including seabirds, cranes and birds of prey, and has spread to some mammals. Scientists have described it as a serious conservation threat as well as an agricultural one. The relationship works in both directions. Wild birds can bring the virus to farms, and large outbreaks among poultry can add to the amount of virus in the environment. This is one reason veterinary agencies ask people to report dead wild birds rather than handle them, and why many countries order poultry to be housed indoors during high-risk periods. Indoor housing reduces contact between domestic flocks and wild birds and their droppings. For readers, the advice is simple. People who find dead or sick wild birds, especially waterbirds or birds of prey, should not touch them and should report them to local veterinary or wildlife authorities. What farmers and bird keepers can do Biosecurity, the set of everyday habits that stop disease getting onto a farm, is the main defence. For commercial farms, that means keeping wild birds out of poultry houses, covering feed and water, changing boots and clothing at the door, cleaning vehicles and limiting visitors. Many outbreaks are traced back to small lapses, such as a gap in a roof or shared equipment moved between sites without cleaning. Backyard keepers matter too. Small flocks that roam outdoors near ponds or wetlands can come into contact with wild ducks and geese. That is why local officials in Biskupiec urged residents to keep domestic birds indoors. Owners who notice sudden deaths, drops in egg laying, or birds that are sluggish or have swollen heads should contact a vet or the local veterinary inspectorate rather than waiting. Some countries have added vaccination to their tools. France, for example, began vaccinating domestic ducks against bird flu in 2023, a step aimed at reducing outbreaks on duck farms. Vaccination can lower the number of infected flocks, but it does not replace biosecurity, and it can complicate trade because importing countries may want proof that vaccinated flocks are free of the virus. The Reuters report on the new French outbreak did not say whether vaccination was relevant to that farm. The cost of each outbreak For farmers, the loss of a flock is a severe blow. A whole house of birds can be gone within days, and restocking usually has to wait until cleaning and disinfection are complete and control zones are lifted. Governments in the EU often compensate farmers for culled birds, but income from lost production and disrupted contracts can still be large. For consumers, the effects show up more slowly, through prices and supply when outbreaks become widespread. Reuters noted that bird flu has disrupted supply and raised food prices in recent years. Is there a risk to people? Neither the Reuters reports nor TVN24 mentioned any human infection linked to these outbreaks. Reuters noted, in general terms, that bird flu has posed a risk of human transmission in recent years, but that was background rather than a finding about these farms. Human cases of H5N1 are rare and have usually involved close, unprotected contact with infected birds or animals. People who work with poultry are generally advised to use protective equipment during culls and clean-up. Properly cooked poultry and eggs are not considered a source of infection. What comes next Veterinary authorities in both countries will be watching for further cases in nearby farms. A first outbreak after a quiet spell, as in Poland, can be followed by others as wild bird migration continues and temperatures drop, conditions in which the virus survives longer in the environment. The coming weeks will show whether these are isolated events or the start of a busy season. Either way, the quick confirmation of both outbreaks through WOAH's reporting system gives farmers and officials across Europe early warning to tighten biosecurity before the virus spreads further. WOAH said 587 turkeys died and the rest of the 18,723 birds were culled. What happened in France? A poultry farm in Pas-de-Calais lost 80 of 4,300 birds to H5N1, and the rest were culled. analysis.time: The outbreaks were confirmed on 23 November 2026, with the Polish outbreak detected in the previous week and the French outbreak detected on the previous Thursday. The article was published on 24 November 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreaks occurred in Poland's Warmian-Masurian region, specifically at a turkey farm in Lipinki, and in northern France, at a poultry farm in the Pas-de-Calais area. The affected population includes turkeys, chickens, and other poultry species.
analysis.event: Highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu outbreaks were confirmed at a turkey farm in Poland and a poultry farm in northern France, as reported by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and cited by Reuters and TVN24.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In Poland, 587 out of 18,723 birds died or were culled, and the farm was part of the country's largest poultry export region. In France, 80 out of 4,300 birds died or were culled. The outbreaks highlight the seasonal spread of the virus and the risk to poultry and wild birds, though no human infections were reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Authorities in Poland and France have implemented procedures to eradicate the disease, including culling flocks, cleaning and disinfecting sites, and setting up control zones. Local officials urged residents to keep domestic birds indoors. The French outbreak's details are based on Reuters reports, and the Polish report did not specify control zones. The situation is under investigation and monitoring.

analysis.brief_en: Highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu outbreaks have been confirmed at a turkey farm in Poland's Warmian-Masurian region and a poultry farm in northern France, according to reports by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and cited by Reuters and TVN24. The Polish outbreak, the first in six months, affected 18,723 birds, with 587 deaths and the rest culled. In France, 80 out of 4,300 birds died or were culled. The outbreaks are linked to autumn bird migration, which increases the risk of transmission from wild birds to poultry. No human infections have been reported in either case. Authorities have taken measures to contain the virus, including culling flocks, cleaning facilities, and urging poultry keepers to maintain biosecurity. Local officials in Poland have advised residents to keep domestic birds indoors. The French outbreak prompted the country to raise its bird flu risk level to 'high,' implementing strict indoor housing rules for poultry. These events underscore the seasonal nature of H5N1 outbreaks and their potential impact on agriculture and conservation.
analysis.summary_en: Highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu outbreaks have been confirmed at a turkey farm in Poland's Warmian-Masurian region and a poultry farm in northern France, according to reports by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and cited by Reuters and TVN24. The Polish outbreak, the first in six months, affected 18,723 birds, with 587 deaths and the rest culled. In France, 80 out of 4,300 birds died or were culled. The outbreaks are linked to autumn bird migration, which increases the risk of transmission from wild birds to poultry. No human infections have been reported in either case. Authorities have taken measures to contain the virus, including culling flocks, cleaning facilities, and urging poultry keepers to maintain biosecurity. Local officials in Poland have advised residents to keep domestic birds indoors. The French outbreak prompted the country to raise its bird flu risk level to 'high,' implementing strict indoor housing rules for poultry. These events underscore the seasonal nature of H5N1 outbreaks and their potential impact on agriculture and conservation.

news.title_zh: 法国报告新 H5N1 暴发 禽流感重返波兰火鸡农场 - 自然世界新闻
news.source_body_en: Highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu outbreaks have been confirmed at a turkey farm in Poland's Warmian-Masurian region and a poultry farm in northern France, according to reports by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and cited by Reuters and TVN24. The Polish outbreak, the first in six months, affected 18,723 birds, with 587 deaths and the rest culled. In France, 80 out of 4,300 birds died or were culled. The outbreaks are linked to autumn bird migration, which increases the risk of transmission from wild birds to poultry. No human infections have been reported in either case. Authorities have taken measures to contain the virus, including culling flocks, cleaning facilities, and urging poultry keepers to maintain biosecurity. Local officials in Poland have advised residents to keep domestic birds indoors. The French outbreak prompted the country to raise its bird flu risk level to 'high,' implementing strict indoor housing rules for poultry. These events underscore the seasonal nature of H5N1 outbreaks and their potential impact on agriculture and conservation.

Murphy) Advertisment17 Share Tweet Fifteen workers at a zoo in central Mexico have developed symptoms after being exposed to H5N1 bird flu, according to local health officials. Two mammals died of the virus at the zoo. The Leon Zoo in Guanajuato state closed on Wednesday as a preventive measure. Zoo director Diana Casillas announced the temporary closure a day earlier, citing recommendations from federal and state health authorities. State health officials identified 29 workers who were exposed, including 15 who developed symptoms. Samples from the workers with symptoms were sent to Mexico’s national reference laboratory for testing. Guanajuato state government secretary Jorge Jimenez Lona said the first five tests on people exposed at the zoo came back negative. More results are expected in the coming days. Article continues below the player Mexico’s animal health agency confirmed that a spider monkey and a tigrillo, a small wild cat, died of H5N1 at the zoo. Another primate is under observation after developing symptoms. The outbreak was traced to wild migratory birds. Three Canada geese died and tested positive for H5N1 before the virus was detected in the mammals. Two wild ducks, a vulture and an ostrich also died. H5N1 primarily infects birds and can also infect mammals. Human infections have occurred in people exposed to infected animals, including poultry and dairy cattle. news.source_body_en: Fifteen workers at the Leon Zoo in Guanajuato, Mexico, developed symptoms after exposure to H5N1 bird flu, according to local health officials. The outbreak was traced to wild migratory birds, and the zoo was temporarily closed as a preventive measure. State health authorities identified 29 workers who were exposed, with the first five tests returning negative. More results are expected in the coming days. The virus also caused the death of two mammals, a spider monkey and a tigrillo, and infected other birds such as Canada geese, wild ducks, a vulture, and an ostrich. The closure was announced by the zoo director, citing recommendations from federal and state health authorities. The situation remains under investigation, with no confirmed risk level yet established.

Reuters Flu season in USA: A sign sits outside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Roybal campus in Atlanta, Georgia, U.S. March 18, 2026. (Reuters Photo) Related Iowa Army Ammunition Plant blast: Controlled detonation of 5 tons of lead azide raises fear, US Army plans evacuation, other major steps Thanksgiving Day-Turkey history, significance: From Thanksgiving dinner table recipe to President's pardon tradition at White House Flu season in the U.S has started days earlier than expected. While many Americans have fallen ill, some are yet to receive mandatory reminder message about vaccine shot. This comes as the World Health Organization said on Tuesday it had been notified by the United States of three confirmed human cases of bird ‌flu in Washington state, including one death. All three cases were adults who worked on dairy farms in Yakima County, Washington state, where the avian influenza virus was recently detected in cattle, the WHO said. WHO said there was no evidence so far of human-to-human transmission based on information available. The first patient developed mild symptoms, including eye irritation and a runny nose, and was not hospitalized. The second, who had underlying medical conditions, developed severe respiratory illness and died on November 1. The third developed conjunctivitis and recovered without hospitalization. Genetic sequencing confirmed all three infections were ‌caused by the H5N1 virus, with strains closely matching those detected in dairy cattle in Washington. High Flu Activity The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before. The CDC also said that more than 3 per cent of doctors’ office visits last week were for flu-like illness, signaling that flu season is really underway. Louisiana is seeing the worst of it so far. The early-season flu activity is higher than what’s usually seen at this point of the year, though it’s not clear that will mean this season will be worse than others, according to CDC’s update. The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season are tied to flu infections. The surge began in the nation’s South and West, and the states seeing high flu activity so far include California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington, according to the CDC. analysis.time: The flu season in the USA started earlier than expected, with high flu activity reported in seven states last week. The three confirmed human cases of H5N1 bird flu were reported in Washington state, with one death occurring on November 1. The CDC's latest update was posted on November 25, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily reported in Washington state, specifically Yakima County, where the avian influenza virus was detected in cattle. The CDC noted that high flu activity is also observed in California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Washington, affecting a significant portion of the population.
analysis.event: These cases were linked to individuals working on dairy farms in Yakima County, where the virus was detected in cattle. The CDC also reported high flu activity in seven states, indicating a broader surge in flu cases.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season are tied to flu infections. The H5N1 cases were confirmed through genetic sequencing, and there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission. However, the early-season flu activity is higher than usual, raising concerns about the potential impact on public health.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC has posted its latest update, and the World Health Organization (WHO) has been notified of the cases. There is no evidence of human-to-human transmission, and the CDC is monitoring the situation. Some individuals have not received mandatory reminders about flu vaccines, indicating potential gaps in public health communication.

analysis.brief_en: The article reports on the early onset of the flu season in the USA, with high flu activity observed in seven states, including Washington, California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas. Three confirmed human cases of H5N1 bird flu were identified in Washington state, with one death, linked to individuals working on dairy farms in Yakima County where the virus was detected in cattle. The CDC noted that more than 3% of doctors’ office visits were for flu-like illness, signaling the flu season is underway. news.title: Antarctic Seabirds Harbor Avian Flu Lineages Linked to South American Outbreaks
news.excerpt: Genomic surveillance of Antarctic seabirds in the South Shetland Islands revealed highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 directly connected to contemporary South American viral lineages.
news.rss_summary_html: Genomic surveillance of Antarctic seabirds in the South Shetland Islands revealed highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 directly connected to contemporary South American viral lineages.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Antarctic Seabirds Harbor Avian Flu Lineages Linked to South American Outbreaks by November 25, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Antarctic Seabirds Harbor Avian Flu Lineages Linked to South American Outbreaks Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram During the 2024–2025 austral summer, field surveillance conducted across seabird breeding colonies in Antarctica confirmed the active circulation of highly pathogenic avian influenza virus subtype H5N1 within resident and migratory wild bird populations. Genomic sequencing and phylogenetic characterization of viral isolates obtained from the South Shetland Islands demonstrated that the circulating pathogens belong to the globally circulating clade 2.3.4.4b. Crucially, evolutionary analysis of complete viral gene segments established that these polar viral sequences share direct genetic connectivity with contemporary South American lineages, including strains detected among marine wildlife along the southern Atlantic coast. The investigation, carried out between November 2024 and January 2025, provides empirical evidence of sustained viral dissemination across southern polar ecosystems and illustrates how intercontinental ecological networks facilitate the introduction of emerging pathogens into dense Antarctic avifauna. The study was designed to evaluate the occurrence, prevalence, and genomic architecture of avian influenza viruses among both resident and wide-ranging seabird species that congregate in the Antarctic Peninsula region. Around one hundred million birds breed in the Antarctic Peninsula during the austral summer, assembling in dense colonies that present favorable conditions for viral transmission. While the Antarctic biome has historically experienced limited contact with foreign pathogens, resulting in native wildlife that generally lacks pre-existing immunological defenses, low-pathogenic avian influenza viruses have previously circulated at low rates of less than five percent. Earlier surveys recorded subtypes such as H11N2 in penguin excreta, followed in 2023 by the detection of subtypes H1N1 and H3N8 on King George Island. However, concerns regarding the introduction of highly pathogenic strains escalated dramatically following the October 2022 emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b in South America, where outbreaks along the Pacific coastline caused severe mortality across wild bird and marine mammal populations. Initial incursions into subantarctic territory were confirmed in late 2023 on Bird Island, South Georgia, followed shortly by detections on the Antarctic mainland, prompting systematic molecular monitoring during the subsequent breeding season. Field collections were carried out during the forty-third Antarctic Operation across diverse seabird nesting sites spanning the South Shetland Islands archipelago, including King George Island, Half Moon Island, Robert Island, Livingston Island, Snow Island, and Nelson Island. The investigative team assembled a total of 278 biological samples collected from four target species: gentoo penguins, chinstrap penguins, southern giant petrels, and south polar skuas. The specimen inventory comprised 166 non-invasive cloacal excreta samples, accompanied by paired sampling from 56 individual birds from which both cloacal swabs and orotracheal swabs were harvested, yielding 56 cloacal swabs and 56 orotracheal swabs. All handling protocols conformed strictly to institutional and international environmental permits alongside biosafety standards established by the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research for managing avian influenza specimens in the Southern Ocean region. Laboratory processing was conducted at the Virology Laboratory within the Institute of Basic Health Sciences at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. Extraction of total ribonucleic acid was executed using the MagMAX CORE extraction kit, configured specifically for complex fecal and biological matrices. Approximately 0.3 grams of collected sample material was suspended in one milliliter of phosphate-buffered saline, homogenized by thorough vortexing, and clarified through centrifugation at 15,000 times gravity for one minute. Supernatant fractions measuring 200 microliters were processed on an automated KingFisher Flex platform, and purified ribonucleic acid was eluted into volumes of 50 microliters before storage at minus eighty degrees Celsius. Complementary deoxyribonucleic acid was subsequently generated using a commercial reverse transcription kit to prepare templates for amplification and molecular identification. Screening for influenza A virus was carried out via real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction targeting a conserved 101-base-pair region of the viral matrix gene using TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix on a QuantStudio 1 real-time PCR platform. Thermal cycling parameters consisted of an initial incubation at 50 degrees Celsius for two minutes, denaturation at 95 degrees Celsius for twenty seconds, and forty cycles comprising 95 degrees Celsius for one second followed by annealing and extension at 60 degrees Celsius for twenty seconds with continuous fluorescence acquisition. Analytical sensitivity was established using a serial nine-point dilution series of a control plasmid containing the matrix gene spanning concentrations from 10 to the ninth power down to 10 to the first power copies per microliter. Quantitative results were evaluated using cycle threshold values, with readings below 30 categorized as representing high viral loads, measurements between 30 and 36 categorized as low positive detections, and values exceeding 36 deemed negative in the absence of a reproducible amplification curve. Primary screening confirmed the presence of influenza A virus matrix gene RNA in 30 out of the 278 evaluated specimens, representing an overall diagnostic positivity of nearly eleven percent across the study area. Viral shedding was observed primarily through digestive pathways, as 25 out of 166 cloacal excreta samples, or approximately 15.1 percent, tested positive, alongside five of the 56 cloacal swabs, or roughly 8.9 percent. In contrast, none of the 56 collected orotracheal swabs yielded positive amplifications, indicating that oral and respiratory shedding was negligible in this sample cohort. Positive specimens were detected in all four investigated avian species, encompassing resident divers such as gentoo penguins and chinstrap penguins, as well as highly dispersive flying seabirds including south polar skuas and southern giant petrels. Furthermore, viral presence was distributed across multiple geographic colonies within the archipelago, confirming that viral dispersal was regionally widespread across the South Shetland Islands rather than confined to a single localized breeding site. Following primary identification, all 30 matrix-positive specimens were screened with a secondary real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assay specific for the H5 hemagglutinin gene, targeting a 131-base-pair amplicon. Eight of the 30 matrix-positive samples, accounting for approximately 26 percent, were confirmed positive for the H5 subtype. To decipher the structural genetics and evolutionary trajectory of these viruses, whole-genome sequencing was executed on two H5-positive isolates using the Ion Torrent sequencing platform. Complete coding sequences for the surface glycoproteins hemagglutinin and neuraminidase were successfully generated from two distinct host species and geographical locations: one gentoo penguin sampled at Hennequin Point on King George Island and one southern giant petrel sampled at Two Summit on Nelson Island. Raw sequence data were processed, assembled, and refined using the Iterative Refinement Meta-Assembler influenza pipeline developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reconstruct reliable consensus sequences. Genomic characterization of the reconstructed sequences confirmed that both Antarctic isolates represent highly pathogenic avian influenza virus subtype H5N1 within clade 2.3.4.4b. Amino acid profiling across the hemagglutinin protein identified a signature polybasic cleavage site motif containing the sequence arginine-glutamic acid-lysine-arginine-arginine-lysine-arginine-glycine-leucine-phenylalanine at the HA1-HA2 junction. The complete coding sequences were formally archived in the GenBank repository, with hemagglutinin sequences cataloged under accession numbers PX919726 for the gentoo penguin isolate and PX919694 for the southern giant petrel isolate, while corresponding neuraminidase sequences were deposited under accession numbers PX919746 and PX919737, respectively. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed using MAFFT alignment, ModelFinder nucleotide substitution model selection, and IQ-TREE with one thousand ultrafast bootstrap iterations to ascertain evolutionary affiliations. Both the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase gene trees revealed that the Antarctic sequences form a robust, well-supported monophyletic cluster nested directly within contemporary South American clade 2.3.4.4b reference strains. Specifically, the Antarctic isolates clustered closely with viral strains identified in South American pinnipeds sampled in Uruguay during 2023, exhibiting node bootstrap support exceeding ninety percent. The congruent phylogenetic topologies observed between the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase segments demonstrate that both surface glycoproteins share an identical evolutionary history without evidence of recent genomic reassortment, indicating a pattern of clonal expansion and southward transmission from continental reservoirs. These genomic and molecular findings substantiate an epidemiological model wherein highly mobile, scavenging seabirds act as bridge hosts that transmit avian influenza viruses from South American coastal habitats across the Southern Ocean into the Antarctic ecosystem. Species such as south polar skuas, which undertake transequatorial migrations, and southern giant petrels, which regularly traverse marine corridors between the Antarctic Peninsula and southern South America, possess movement dynamics suited for introducing continental viral lineages into naive breeding colonies. Following introduction, high colony densities facilitate local transmission among resident species like gentoo and chinstrap penguins. The investigation, carried out between November 2024 and January 2025, provides empirical evidence of sustained viral dissemination across southern polar ecosystems and illustrates how intercontinental ecological networks facilitate the introduction of emerging pathogens into dense Antarctic avifauna. The study was designed to evaluate the occurrence, prevalence, and genomic architecture of avian influenza viruses among both resident and wide-ranging seabird species that congregate in the Antarctic Peninsula region. Around one hundred million birds breed in the Antarctic Peninsula during the austral summer, assembling in dense colonies that present favorable conditions for viral transmission. While the Antarctic biome has historically experienced limited contact with foreign pathogens, resulting in native wildlife that generally lacks pre-existing immunological defenses, low-pathogenic avian influenza viruses have previously circulated at low rates of less than five percent. Earlier surveys recorded subtypes such as H11N2 in penguin excreta, followed in 2023 by the detection of subtypes H1N1 and H3N8 on King George Island. However, concerns regarding the introduction of highly pathogenic strains escalated dramatically following the October 2022 emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b in South America, where outbreaks along the Pacific coastline caused severe mortality across wild bird and marine mammal populations. Initial incursions into subantarctic territory were confirmed in late 2023 on Bird Island, South Georgia, followed shortly by detections on the Antarctic mainland, prompting systematic molecular monitoring during the subsequent breeding season. Field collections were carried out during the forty-third Antarctic Operation across diverse seabird nesting sites spanning the South Shetland Islands archipelago, including King George Island, Half Moon Island, Robert Island, Livingston Island, Snow Island, and Nelson Island. The investigative team assembled a total of 278 biological samples collected from four target species: gentoo penguins, chinstrap penguins, southern giant petrels, and south polar skuas. The specimen inventory comprised 166 non-invasive cloacal excreta samples, accompanied by paired sampling from 56 individual birds from which both cloacal swabs and orotracheal swabs were harvested, yielding 56 cloacal swabs and 56 orotracheal swabs. All handling protocols conformed strictly to institutional and international environmental permits alongside biosafety standards established by the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research for managing avian influenza specimens in the Southern Ocean region. Laboratory processing was conducted at the Virology Laboratory within the Institute of Basic Health Sciences at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. Extraction of total ribonucleic acid was executed using the MagMAX CORE extraction kit, configured specifically for complex fecal and biological matrices. Approximately 0.3 grams of collected sample material was suspended in one milliliter of phosphate-buffered saline, homogenized by thorough vortexing, and clarified through centrifugation at 15,000 times gravity for one minute. Supernatant fractions measuring 200 microliters were processed on an automated KingFisher Flex platform, and purified ribonucleic acid was eluted into volumes of 50 microliters before storage at minus eighty degrees Celsius. Complementary deoxyribonucleic acid was subsequently generated using a commercial reverse transcription kit to prepare templates for amplification and molecular identification. Screening for influenza A virus was carried out via real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction targeting a conserved 101-base-pair region of the viral matrix gene using TaqMan Fast Advanced Master Mix on a QuantStudio 1 real-time PCR platform. Thermal cycling parameters consisted of an initial incubation at 50 degrees Celsius for two minutes, denaturation at 95 degrees Celsius for twenty seconds, and forty cycles comprising 95 degrees Celsius for one second followed by annealing and extension at 60 degrees Celsius for twenty seconds with continuous fluorescence acquisition. Analytical sensitivity was established using a serial nine-point dilution series of a control plasmid containing the matrix gene spanning concentrations from 10 to the ninth power down to 10 to the first power copies per microliter. Quantitative results were evaluated using cycle threshold values, with readings below 30 categorized as representing high viral loads, measurements between 30 and 36 categorized as low positive detections, and values exceeding 36 deemed negative in the absence of a reproducible amplification curve. Primary screening confirmed the presence of influenza A virus matrix gene RNA in 30 out of the 278 evaluated specimens, representing an overall diagnostic positivity of nearly eleven percent across the study area. Viral shedding was observed primarily through digestive pathways, as 25 out of 166 cloacal excreta samples, or approximately 15.1 percent, tested positive, alongside five of the 56 cloacal swabs, or roughly 8.9 percent. In contrast, none of the 56 collected orotracheal swabs yielded positive amplifications, indicating that oral and respiratory shedding was negligible in this sample cohort. Positive specimens were detected in all four investigated avian species, encompassing resident divers such as gentoo penguins and chinstrap penguins, as well as highly dispersive flying seabirds including south polar skuas and southern giant petrels. Furthermore, viral presence was distributed across multiple geographic colonies within the archipelago, confirming that viral dispersal was regionally widespread across the South Shetland Islands rather than confined to a single localized breeding site. Following primary identification, all 30 matrix-positive specimens were screened with a secondary real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assay specific for the H5 hemagglutinin gene, targeting a 131-base-pair amplicon. Eight of the 30 matrix-positive samples, accounting for approximately 26 percent, were confirmed positive for the H5 subtype. To decipher the structural genetics and evolutionary trajectory of these viruses, whole-genome sequencing was executed on two H5-positive isolates using the Ion Torrent sequencing platform. Complete coding sequences for the surface glycoproteins hemagglutinin and neuraminidase were successfully generated from two distinct host species and geographical locations: one gentoo penguin sampled at Hennequin Point on King George Island and one southern giant petrel sampled at Two Summit on Nelson Island. Raw sequence data were processed, assembled, and refined using the Iterative Refinement Meta-Assembler influenza pipeline developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reconstruct reliable consensus sequences. Genomic characterization of the reconstructed sequences confirmed that both Antarctic isolates represent highly pathogenic avian influenza virus subtype H5N1 within clade 2.3.4.4b. Amino acid profiling across the hemagglutinin protein identified a signature polybasic cleavage site motif containing the sequence arginine-glutamic acid-lysine-arginine-arginine-lysine-arginine-glycine-leucine-phenylalanine at the HA1-HA2 junction. The complete coding sequences were formally archived in the GenBank repository, with hemagglutinin sequences cataloged under accession numbers PX919726 for the gentoo penguin isolate and PX919694 for the southern giant petrel isolate, while corresponding neuraminidase sequences were deposited under accession numbers PX919746 and PX919737, respectively. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed using MAFFT alignment, ModelFinder nucleotide substitution model selection, and IQ-TREE with one thousand ultrafast bootstrap iterations to ascertain evolutionary affiliations. Both the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase gene trees revealed that the Antarctic sequences form a robust, well-supported monophyletic cluster nested directly within contemporary South American clade 2.3.4.4b reference strains. Specifically, the Antarctic isolates clustered closely with viral strains identified in South American pinnipeds sampled in Uruguay during 2023, exhibiting node bootstrap support exceeding ninety percent. The congruent phylogenetic topologies observed between the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase segments demonstrate that both surface glycoproteins share an identical evolutionary history without evidence of recent genomic reassortment, indicating a pattern of clonal expansion and southward transmission from continental reservoirs. These genomic and molecular findings substantiate an epidemiological model wherein highly mobile, scavenging seabirds act as bridge hosts that transmit avian influenza viruses from South American coastal habitats across the Southern Ocean into the Antarctic ecosystem. Species such as south polar skuas, which undertake transequatorial migrations, and southern giant petrels, which regularly traverse marine corridors between the Antarctic Peninsula and southern South America, possess movement dynamics suited for introducing continental viral lineages into naive breeding colonies. Following introduction, high colony densities facilitate local transmission among resident species like gentoo and chinstrap penguins. analysis.location_and_population: India, through the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), with focus on agricultural research institutes and farming communities.
analysis.event: India’s first indigenous H5N1 Avian Influenza vaccine was developed by ICAR-NIHSAD, Bhopal, and is a significant breakthrough in agricultural science. The event is confirmed as a development, not an outbreak.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The vaccine development is a major scientific achievement with potential to enhance disease control in poultry and reduce zoonotic risks. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The development is confirmed, with no indication of ongoing investigation or uncertainty. The source is an official statement from ICAR.

analysis.brief_en: On November 24, 2026, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) announced the development of India’s first indigenous H5N1 Avian Influenza vaccine by its National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD) in Bhopal. This breakthrough marks a significant advancement in the country’s agricultural science and disease control capabilities. The vaccine is designed to combat highly pathogenic avian influenza, which poses risks to poultry and can lead to zoonotic infections in humans. The development is confirmed as an official achievement, with no reported outbreak or specific case numbers mentioned. ICAR emphasizes the importance of such innovations in safeguarding both animal and human health, particularly in the context of avian-origin zoonotic infections. The vaccine’s creation is part of broader efforts to enhance agricultural resilience and public health preparedness.

news.source_body_en: On November 24, 2026, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) announced the development of India’s first indigenous H5N1 Avian Influenza vaccine by its National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (ICAR-NIHSAD) in Bhopal. news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 24 日,印度农业研究委员会 (ICAR) 宣布其位于博帕尔的国家高安全动物疾病研究所 (ICAR-NIHSAD) 开发出印度首个本土 H5N1 禽流感 疫苗。这一突破标志着我国农业科技和病害防治能力取得重大进步。疫苗 旨在对抗 高致病性禽流感,高致病性禽流感 对家禽构成风险,并可能导致人类人畜共患感染。该开发已被确认为官方成果,但没有报告 暴发 或提及具体案例编号。ICAR 强调此类创新对于保障动物和人类健康的重要性,特别是在禽源人畜共患感染的情况下。疫苗 的创建是增强农业复原力和公共卫生准备工作的更广泛努力的一部分。

news.content_title: Bird Flu in Crows Triggers 12 km Alert Zone in Bihar
news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Bird Flu in Crows Triggers 12 km Alert Zone in Bihar By Elias Reed Published: Nov 23 2026, 9:54 AM EST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail INDRANIL MUKHERJEE/AFP via Getty Images Four crows found dead at the official residence of the district magistrate in Biharsharif, the main town of Nalanda district in the Indian state of Bihar, have tested positive for the H5N1 strain of bird flu, local media reported on Sunday, 22 November 2026. The crows were found on 6 November inside the district magistrate's residence complex, Amar Ujala reported. Samples were sent to laboratories in Patna and Kolkata and finally to the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases in Bhopal, India's top laboratory for dangerous animal diseases, which confirmed H5N1. A rapid response team has been formed, and leave for all district veterinarians and animal husbandry staff has been cancelled with immediate effect so they are available for emergencies. Poultry farms within 12 km are under surveillance, with chicken samples being collected for testing. Block-level teams are monitoring poultry farms and bird movements in rural areas, Amar Ujala said. District Animal Husbandry Officer Dr. Rekha Choubey said no poultry farm in the district had confirmed bird flu and no abnormal chicken deaths had been reported, ETV Bharat said. Officials described this as a relief. How did crows get bird flu? Officials suspect the virus arrived with migratory birds. Large numbers of migratory birds and ducks arrive at the district's reservoirs at this time of year, and officials said the crows may have been infected through contact with infected birds, First Bihar reported. Dr. Choubey said the crows may have caught the virus from migratory birds and ducks arriving from Siberia and other cold regions, according to Amar Ujala. This is a suspicion, not a confirmed finding. Crows are scavengers that feed on carcasses, rubbish and food scraps. That habit can expose them to the virus if they eat dead or sick birds. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Symptoms Study Biology Home Health Researchers Identify Novel Avian Influenza Virus in Chinese Poultry Researchers Identify Novel Avian Influenza Virus in Chinese Poultry Ashley Morgan Published Nov 24, 2026 - 02:48 4 Reads Last Update Nov 24, 2026 - 02:48 Share WhatsApp Outbreak Smallest Font Largest Font Veterinary researchers have identified a previously undocumented avian influenza virus in commercial poultry in Shangqiu, Henan Province, China, after investigating a severe respiratory disease outbreak in December 2025. The virus, designated A/chicken/Henan/NL04/2025 or NL04, belongs to the low-pathogenic H6N2 subtype but carries an unusual genetic combination associated with multiple avian influenza lineages. According to research published by bioengineer.org on November 23, 2026, the outbreak affected a commercial layer flock consisting of 54-week-old chickens. The infection caused severe respiratory symptoms and a cumulative mortality rate of 15 percent. Infected birds experienced elevated body temperatures, extreme lethargy, reduced feed consumption, and breathing difficulties. Some chickens died within three to four days after symptoms appeared. Postmortem examinations revealed substantial airway obstruction caused by long, white, mucus-like plugs inside the bronchial passages. Researchers identified these obstructions as the primary cause of suffocation and death. The examinations also detected yolk sac peritonitis, with lesions more severe than those typically associated with low-pathogenic avian influenza. Whole-genome sequencing revealed that NL04 combines genetic material from different avian influenza lineages. Its hemagglutinin gene originated from a waterfowl-associated H6 lineage, while its neuraminidase gene came from the poultry-associated H9N2 lineage. The six internal gene segments, identified as PB2, PB1, PA, NP, M, and NS, originated from the chicken-adapted H9N2 G57 genotype. Their nucleotide sequence identities ranged from 96.38 percent to 99.12 percent. Researchers also identified several molecular characteristics associated with viral replication, host adaptation, and antiviral resistance. These included the S31N substitution in the matrix 2 protein, which is associated with resistance to adamantane antiviral drugs, including amantadine. Despite these genetic characteristics, the virus retained a hemagglutinin cleavage site consistent with low-pathogenic avian influenza. Researchers also found that the canonical mammalian receptor-binding mutations Q226L and G228S were absent. To investigate the virus's biological behavior, researchers conducted experiments involving two-week-old specific-pathogen-free chickens. The birds received an infectious dose of 10^6.0 EID50 through combined ocular and intranasal inoculation. Unlike the commercial flock in Henan, all experimentally infected chickens survived the 14-day observation period. They showed no obvious clinical symptoms, including fever, depression, lethargy, or diarrhea. Their weight gain also showed no statistically significant difference compared with uninfected control animals. However, microscopic examinations revealed significant tissue damage despite the absence of obvious clinical illness. Tracheal samples showed extensive loss of epithelial cilia, while lung examinations identified alveolar atrophy and inflammatory cell infiltration. Researchers also detected kidney abnormalities, including glomerular epithelial cell shrinkage and infiltration by red and white blood cells. Immunohistochemical testing confirmed viral nucleoprotein antigen in lung alveolar epithelial cells, providing evidence of viral replication in respiratory tissues. Viral measurements taken three days after infection showed the highest concentrations in the upper respiratory tract and associated ocular tissues. Nasal turbinate samples reached 10^5.56 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter, while the Harderian gland recorded 10^4.23 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter. Both tracheal and bronchial samples recorded viral concentrations of 10^1.82 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter. These findings demonstrated that NL04 primarily replicated in respiratory tissues under the experimental conditions. The contrasting outcomes between the commercial flock and laboratory-infected chickens highlight a substantial difference in disease severity under different production conditions. The commercial outbreak produced 15 percent mortality, whereas experimentally infected chickens survived the entire monitoring period without apparent clinical illness. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, November 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Novel Avian Influenza Reassortant Virus Discovered in Chinese Poultry Outbreak by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Novel Avian Influenza Reassortant Virus Discovered in Chinese Poultry Outbreak Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Veterinary researchers investigating an acute respiratory disease outbreak in commercial poultry in central China have identified and characterized a novel reassortant avian influenza virus designated A/chicken/Henan/NL04/2025, or NL04. The natural reassortant belongs to the low-pathogenic H6N2 subtype but carries an unusual genetic composition that combines external and internal gene segments from divergent avian influenza lineages. The outbreak occurred in December 2025 within a fifty-four-week-old commercial layer flock located in Shangqiu, Henan Province, causing severe respiratory symptoms and a fifteen percent cumulative mortality rate. Affected birds exhibited severe clinical signs including elevated body temperature, profound lethargy, reduced feed intake, neck extension during respiration, and acute death within three to four days of onset. Postmortem examinations of affected field birds showed severe bronchial obstruction caused by long white exudative plugs occluding the airways, which investigators identified as the primary cause of suffocation and death. Additional necropsy findings in the field flock revealed signs of yolk sac peritonitis, presenting a lesion severity substantially greater than that typically documented during standard low-pathogenic avian influenza infections. Whole-genome sequencing of the isolated NL04 strain revealed an intricate reassortment profile that integrates segments from two major circulating avian influenza lineages. The hemagglutinin gene was traced to a waterfowl-origin H6 lineage showing 96.59 percent nucleotide identity to known sequences and clustering within Eurasian group I, also designated the ST339-like lineage. In contrast, the neuraminidase gene derived from an H9N2 poultry lineage, exhibiting 99.37 percent nucleotide homology with contemporary circulating H9N2 isolates and falling within the Eurasian Y280-like lineage. Crucially, all six internal gene segments—PB2, PB1, PA, NP, M, and NS—were inherited from the chicken-adapted H9N2 G57 genotype, exhibiting high nucleotide identities between 96.38 percent and 99.12 percent. While initial sequence alignment identified top basic local alignment matches for the PB2 and M genes in H3N3 and H3N8 isolates, phylogenetic analyses demonstrated that those matching segments were themselves derived from circulating H9N2 G57 viruses. This genomic constellation demonstrates that NL04 did not acquire its internal segments through piecemeal genetic drift, but rather inherited an intact ribonucleoprotein cassette and structural core that is widely established in terrestrial poultry. Analysis of molecular virulence markers in the primary sequences revealed critical structural attributes governing host range, drug susceptibility, and baseline pathogenicity. The hemagglutinin cleavage site of the NL04 isolate possessed the sequence PQIETR↓G, lacking the consecutive basic amino acids that characterize highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses and thereby confirming its classification as a low-pathogenic strain. The canonical mammalian receptor-binding mutations Q226L and G228S were absent in the hemagglutinin protein, with residues Q226 and G228 fully preserved. However, analysis of the neuraminidase protein identified a deletion within the stalk region spanning residues 62 to 64, a structural change that has previously been linked to elevated virulence in mammalian hosts, alongside a K368N substitution associated with immune escape and antigenic drift. Within the matrix 2 protein, the isolate harbored the S31N substitution, which confers pharmacological resistance to the adamantane class of antiviral drugs, specifically amantadine. Discover more Check Symptoms Get Cold Relief Study Biology Order DNA Kits Buy Fresh Poultry The six internal gene products contained numerous non-canonical substitutions previously documented to enhance polymerase activity and replication kinetics in distinct genetic backgrounds. The PB2 protein carried the specific substitutions A588V, T598I, and A676T, all associated with heightened viral replication and polymerase efficiency in experimental models, while lacking the canonical mammalian adaptive markers A199S, I292V, and E627K. In the PB1 protein, residues 473V and I368V were present, mutations linked respectively to enhanced polymerase performance in mammalian cell systems and respiratory droplet transmissibility in ferrets. The polymerase acidic subunit contained K356R, associated with enhanced mammalian replication, alongside the avian-mammalian species marker S409N. Further markers were detected in the nucleoprotein, where L3S was identified, and in the matrix 1 protein, which exhibited the species signature T215A and the virulence-associated change N30D. Finally, the non-structural protein NS1 carried four recognized substitutions—P42S, E172K, N205S, and P212S—known to modify virulence and interferon antagonism in mammalian experimental hosts. To rigorously determine the intrinsic biological behavior of the isolate without the confounding environmental variables of intensive farming, researchers inoculated two-week-old specific-pathogen-free chickens via combined ocular and intranasal routes using an infectious dose of 10^6.0 EID50. In stark contrast to the devastating fifteen percent mortality recorded in the commercial Henan flock, all inoculated specific-pathogen-free chickens survived the full fourteen-day experimental monitoring period. The infected birds displayed no overt clinical abnormalities, remaining free of fever, depression, lethargy, or diarrheal illness, and their body weight gain showed no statistically significant difference when compared with uninfected phosphate-buffered saline control animals. Gross pathological evaluation performed at three days post-infection showed only subtle organ changes, including focal hemorrhagic spots within the Harderian gland, mild enlargement and petechial hemorrhages in the thymus, and slight bursal swelling with minor mucoid exudation, while respiratory organs such as the trachea and lungs showed no macroscopic lesions. Despite the lack of overt clinical illness and visible macroscopic pathology in experimental chickens, microscopic histopathological evaluation revealed extensive underlying tissue damage throughout the respiratory tract. Examination of hematoxylin and eosin-stained tracheal sections demonstrated severe ciliary shedding along the epithelial lining without overt hemorrhagic extravasation. In lung sections, alveolar atrophy was prominent and accompanied by substantial infiltration of inflammatory cells into interstitial spaces, while kidney tissues showed glomerular epithelial karyopyknosis with erythrocyte and leukocyte infiltration. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed viral replication in the respiratory epithelium, revealing abundant viral nucleoprotein antigen in lung alveolar epithelial cells. Semi-quantitative histopathological scoring confirmed that tissue lesions were most severe in the lungs and trachea, followed by the kidneys. Quantitative viral titration of tissues at three days post-infection established that viral replication peaked in the upper respiratory tract and associated ocular tissues, reaching 10^5.56 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter in the nasal turbinates and 10^4.23 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter in the Harderian gland, while trachea and bronchus titers both reached 10^1.82 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter, confirming strict respiratory tropism. The marked discrepancy between mild experimental laboratory infections in specific-pathogen-free chickens and the severe mortality observed in the commercial Henan flock highlights the profound influence of secondary production factors. In industrial poultry operations, high-density stocking, environmental ammonia accumulation, ventilation stress, and concurrent microbial exposures create an environment highly permissive to exacerbated clinical disease. Primary viral replication by low-pathogenic strains such as NL04 damages the respiratory ciliated epithelium and compromises mucociliary clearance, rendering birds highly vulnerable to secondary opportunistic bacterial invaders such as Escherichia coli and Mycoplasma species. These secondary pathogens frequently induce severe exudative fibrinous airsacculitis and bronchial occlusion, explaining the fatal plugs observed in the commercial outbreak. The experimental findings emphasize that specific-pathogen-free animal trials alone cannot predict the true veterinary and economic impact of emerging avian influenza variants in real-world commercial poultry operations. To evaluate potential mammalian spillover risk, the research team intranasally challenged six-week-old female BALB/c mice with 10^6.00 EID50 of the purified NL04 virus. Over the fourteen-day evaluation period, all infected mice survived without displaying detectable respiratory distress, ruffled fur, or statistically significant weight loss relative to sham-inoculated controls. Organ titration at three days post-infection demonstrated limited replication, with viral titers confined predominantly to the upper respiratory tract at 10^3.25 EID50 per 0.1 milliliter in nasal turbinates, accompanied by minimal levels of 10^1.56 in lung tissue and 10^1.18 in kidney tissue. Brain samples showed no viral replication, and histological sections revealed only mild alveolar inflammatory infiltration without structural necrosis. In vitro replication kinetics comparing Madin-Darby canine kidney cells and primary chick embryo fibroblasts revealed rapid viral propagation in both cell types, though avian fibroblasts supported significantly higher viral yields during early replication phases between 12 and 48 hours post-infection. These mammalian studies demonstrate that despite bearing several molecular adaptation markers, NL04 possesses limited mammalian replication competence and low intrinsic pathogenicity in mice. Global epidemiological analysis of 5,029 historical H6Ny avian influenza isolates cataloged from 1963 to 2025 provided broader context on subtype evolution, ecological reservoirs, and interspecies transmission events. Annual isolation numbers remained low through the late 1990s before expanding sharply into an ongoing elevated circulation plateau that peaked in 2014 with approximately 440 recorded isolates. Avian species constituted the predominant ecological niche, representing 91.7 percent of the total dataset, whereas environmental samples accounted for 6.4 percent, and mammalian and human isolations remained exceptionally scarce at four and two cases respectively. Among the nine recognized neuraminidase pairings, H6N2 and H6N6 emerged as the dominant subtypes globally, accounting for 30.98 percent and 28.08 percent of all isolates, followed by H6N1 at 17.24 percent. While wild aquatic waterfowl constitute the natural ancestral reservoir, the surveillance dataset documented 145 separate spillover events of H6N2 into domestic chickens, demonstrating that terrestrial poultry now represent an established secondary niche that facilitates frequent encounters and reassortment with endemic poultry viruses. Given the commercial risks posed by circulating reassortants, the researchers formulated and tested a whole-inactivated oil-emulsion vaccine candidate derived from the homologous NL04 strain. Purified allantoic virus was inactivated using 0.1 percent beta-propiolactone for 24 hours at four degrees Celsius, followed by beta-propiolactone hydrolysis at thirty-seven degrees Celsius and high-speed emulsification with Montanide ISA 78 VG adjuvant. Three-week-old specific-pathogen-free chickens received a single intramuscular injection of 0.3 milliliters of the prepared vaccine formulation, with control animals receiving adjuvant-emulsified saline. Serum hemagglutination inhibition titers monitored weekly reached a mean of 13.25 log2 by five weeks post-immunization, confirming the induction of a potent humoral immune response. Following homologous live virus challenge at five weeks, vaccinated birds exhibited a substantially shortened and restricted shedding profile, shedding virus exclusively through the oral route and clearing infection within four days, whereas unvaccinated control birds shed virus predominantly through the oral route across the first week post-challenge. Neutralization assays conducted in embryonated chicken eggs further demonstrated that post-vaccination antisera effectively neutralized the homologous NL04 virus and exhibited cross-protective neutralizing activity against a heterologous H6N1 isolate collected from poultry in December 2025. In both cases, incubation of serum-virus mixtures abolished detectable hemagglutinating activity in harvested allantoic fluid, confirming that vaccine-induced antibodies recognize shared antigenic epitopes across distinct H6 lineages. The investigators identified key study limitations, including the lack of quantitative in vitro receptor-binding assays, the absence of aerosol droplet transmission experiments, the reliance on a single field isolate, and the need for vaccine efficacy validation under commercial field conditions with secondary pathogens. Nonetheless, the investigation underscores that the continuous genetic exchange between waterfowl-origin surface glycoproteins and the robust H9N2 G57 internal ribonucleoprotein machinery produces resilient reassortants capable of threatening commercial poultry health, highlighting the urgent need for sustained poultry genomic surveillance.
